why: קַדְמַת appears 6 times in the Hebrew Old Testament across 3 books.
Primarily functions as: p (5×), c (1×).

prose.def: The state of being former or ancient — what something was before, its earlier condition or remote past.
prose.article: קַדְמַת carries the sense of priority in time — the 'before' state of something, whether a distant past era or a previously held condition. Its six occurrences cluster in Ezekiel (4 times), where it appears notably in Ezekiel 16:55 describing the restoration of cities to their 'former estate,' and once each in Psalms and Isaiah. The LXX is fascinatingly split: ancient translators sometimes chose ἀποκαθίστημι, a word meaning 'restoration to a former state,' and sometimes πρωΐα, meaning 'early morning' or 'former time' — suggesting some ambiguity even among ancient readers about whether the word stressed restoration or simply earliness. The KJV range of 'afore,' 'antiquity,' and 'former estate' reflects this same tension between a temporal marker and a description of a prior condition.
prose.caution: Confidence is rated low, the word occurs only 6 times across 3 books, and the split LXX rendering between 'restoration' and 'early/former time' indicates genuine ancient uncertainty about the word's precise nuance.

prose.def: An Aramaic word meaning 'former time' or 'previously,' referring to an earlier period or past practice.
prose.article: This Aramaic term appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in late books with Aramaic sections: Ezra and Daniel. It carries the sense of 'before' or 'in earlier times,' pointing back to a prior state or established custom. The KJV renders it as 'aforetime' and 'ago,' capturing its straightforward temporal meaning. Its occurrence in both a historical decree context (Ezra 5:11) and a narrative about Daniel's prayer habits (Daniel 6:11) confirms it simply marks continuity with a previous practice.
prose.caution: With only 2 occurrences in the entire OT and a low confidence rating, this Aramaic word has very sparse attestation, limiting certainty about its full range of use.

prose.def: A personal name — the youngest son of Ishmael, listed among the twelve Ishmaelite tribal leaders.
prose.article: Kedemah is the name of the youngest of Ishmael's twelve sons, appearing in the genealogical lists of Genesis 25:15 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 1:31. The KJV renders it consistently as 'Kedemah' in both occurrences, and the name appears only in these two parallel passages. Strong's connects the name to the root meaning 'precedence' or 'eastward,' but in the text it functions purely as a proper name for a tribal ancestor.
prose.caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in parallel genealogical lists, virtually nothing can be said about this figure beyond the name itself; any meaning drawn from the underlying root remains speculative.

why: קַדְמוֹנָה appears 1 time in the Hebrew Old Testament across 1 book.
Primarily functions as: a (1×).
Hapax legomenon — occurs only once; range of meaning inferred from context and ancient versions.

prose.def: An adjective meaning 'eastern,' referring to direction toward the east.
prose.article: קַדְמוֹנָה appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 47:8, where it describes the direction of a river flowing eastward in Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple. The word derives from the root קָדַם, which relates to what is 'in front' or 'before,' since east was understood as the direction one faces. The KJV consistently renders it 'east,' and the term functions as an adjective modifying direction. Its single occurrence makes it a hapax legomenon with a straightforward geographic meaning.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making contextual comparison impossible, though its derivation from the well-attested root קָדַם strongly supports the 'eastern' meaning.

why: קַדְמוֹנִי appears 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament across 7 books.
Primarily functions as: a (8×), adjective (2×).

prose.def: An adjective meaning 'former' or 'eastern,' referring either to what is ancient in time or what lies to the east in space.
prose.article: קַדְמוֹנִי carries a double orientation: backward in time (ancient, former) and eastward in space (oriental). Both senses flow from the same Hebrew root concept of 'what is in front,' since in ancient Israelite orientation, east was the direction one faced. With only 10 occurrences across 7 books, the word is relatively rare; Ezekiel uses it most (4×), largely in the spatial sense of 'the east gate.' The LXX renders it as πρῶτος ('first') three times and ἀρχαῖος ('ancient') twice, confirming that Greek translators primarily saw the temporal sense as dominant.
prose.caution: One LXX rendering translates this word as Γώγ (Gog), which is highly unusual and suggests either a textual variant or a very puzzling interpretive choice; this specific instance carries genuine uncertainty.

prose.def: A place name in eastern Palestine (Moab region), possibly meaning 'eastern places' or 'beginnings.'
prose.article: Kedemoth is a location in the territory east of the Jordan River, appearing 4 times across Deuteronomy, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles. In Deuteronomy 2:26 it names a wilderness from which Moses sent messengers to Sihon; in Joshua it appears as a Levitical city assigned within the tribe of Reuben. The KJV translates it exclusively as the proper name 'Kedemoth' in every occurrence, offering no window into its underlying meaning beyond the name itself.
prose.caution: The exact location of Kedemoth is archaeologically unconfirmed, and whether the name carries a meaningful sense of 'eastern places' or 'beginnings' from the root qadam is uncertain rather than established.

prose.def: An Aramaic adjective meaning 'first' in sequence or rank, used to describe the earliest or foremost among a series.
prose.article: This Aramaic word appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, all in Daniel 7, where it describes the 'first' of the visionary beasts in Daniel's night vision. Its meaning is narrow and consistent — it simply marks something as first in a sequence. The LXX evidence aligns with this straightforward reading, and the KJV translates it uniformly as 'first' across all occurrences.
prose.caution: This is an Aramaic loanword with only 3 attestations confined to a single chapter, making its full semantic range difficult to assess with confidence.
